idiom_name: ASP.NET Core output formatters + Razor view engines with content negotiation
implementation_notes: One action returns the model and the framework selects the representation: ObjectResult consults the client Accept header and asks each registered IOutputFormatter in turn (System.Text.Json by default; XML after AddXmlSerializerFormatters(); a custom IOutputFormatter adds CSV or PDF), while Razor view engines produce the HTML representation through ViewResult and IViewEngine. The classic view registry therefore becomes DI-registered formatters plus view-engine registration, and the per-format code you still write is exactly the non-built-in representation. Returning JsonResult or ContentResult directly is the right move when one representation must be pinned deliberately, not as the default wiring.
pitfalls: ASP.NET Core ignores the browser Accept header unless MvcOptions.RespectBrowserAcceptHeader is enabled, so 'negotiation works in curl but not in Chrome' is expected configuration, not a framework bug.
Serializing the EF entity directly pulls navigation properties into the payload and can trigger lazy-loading or cycle errors; return a DTO and keep the entity out of the formatter.
HTML and API drift apart quietly: a property added to the entity but not to MovieDto appears in the Razor view only, and nothing fails.
